title: Classified N.S.A. Network Goes Down, Causing Work Disruptions
summary: There are currently no signs that the outage is the result of a cyberattack or other nefarious activity, according to people familiar with the matter.

The National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network was offline Tuesday, prompting the spy agency to tell its work force to stagger arrivals at its Maryland headquarters, according to people familiar with the matter.


The network, known as NSANet, is central to the agency’s work, according to current and former intelligence officials. It is used to send and receive top secret information. Much of the work that the agency conducts — including surveilling foreign spies and terrorists — is classified, so a disruption of the network would be a severe impediment.


There are currently no signs that the outage is the result of a cyberattack or other nefarious activity, the people said. NSANet has been unstable for weeks, one of the people said, which has fueled frustration within the work force.[CNN earlier reported](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/17/politics/highly-classified-national-security-communications-network-goes-down) the outage.


The issue Tuesday appeared to be caused by a need to patch software with a system update, according to one person. It was not clear what software was at issue.


The disruption is the latest in a cascade of recent technology failures that have grabbed headlines in recent days, including a nationwide[grounding of flights](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/13/us/ground-stop-nationwide-flights-faa) , an[outage of Microsoft products](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/microsoft-outage-what-to-know.html) and interruptions to[banking services](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/bank-outages-down.html) . None of those episodes have been linked to a cyberattack and have instead been blamed on routine technology issues.


“Even if this particular situation at the N.S.A. is not nefarious in nature, this certainly highlights the concern that everyone has around aging digital infrastructure that feels more top of mind than ever,” said Bryson Byrd, a cybersecurity adviser at Huntress, a U.S.-based digital security firm. “It’s easy to put on a tinfoil hat and speculate about why all these outages are happening. But you don’t need a cyberattack to bring operations to a halt.”


A voice mail call box for National Security Agency employees reached by a New York Times reporter on Tuesday morning referred to the disruption as a “code yellow,” or the second-highest warning in a three-tier system, for the day shift at the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Md.


“Nonemergency personnel should begin staggered arrival no earlier than noon,” the recording said. “Emergency personnel to report for duty as scheduled.”


The N.S.A. did not immediately respond to a request for comment.


The National Security Agency is one of the largest intelligence agencies in the U.S. government, with a work force of tens of thousands. It is the lead spy agency responsible for collecting signals intelligence, or electronic intercepts, of foreign communications for U.S. policymakers, and it plays a central role in overseeing the cybersecurity of government networks.


Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.
